title: Say where it came from
hookLine: why we always name the source: each story belongs to the people who kept it
carry: a teaching with no address can't be visited

lines: A SUNSET AND A CURLY FONT.
WHY I ALWAYS NAME THE SOURCE.
cards: You've seen them. A sunset photo, a lovely sentence in a curly font, and underneath: Buddha. Or Rumi.
Or Einstein. It gets shared again and again. And sometimes the person named never said it.
Nobody's exactly lying. Someone liked a line, a well-known name made it feel truer, and it drifted loose from wherever it started.
Every day on this path, i say where a story came from, sometimes fussily: chapter and verse, which collection, who wrote it down, and when. Today is about why.

teach.h: HONESTY: NO WORDS IN THEIR MOUTHS.
teach.b: Three reasons. First, honesty. On day twenty-one i mentioned a well-known Rumi line about a field beyond ideas of right and wrong.
The popular wording is a modern English version: beautiful, but not a translation you can check line by line against what Rumi wrote in Persian. So i said so.
Some quotes online signed by the Buddha appear in no Buddhist text at all. Saying where something came from keeps you from putting words in someone's mouth.
Second, gratitude. Every story on this path was kept by somebody, often at a cost. Sufi writers like Attar kept the stories of Rabia.

The desert monks' sayings passed from elder to student until someone wrote them down. Sikh families passed down the stories of Guru Nanak. Hasidic communities kept the tales of their rebbes and told them again and again.
Saying this is a Hasidic tale, or this comes from the Janamsakhis, is a thank-you to the people who carried it here. The stories aren't mine. I'm a guest.

teach.h: A MAP: WHERE TO LEARN MORE.
teach.b: Know a story's home and you know where to learn more, and whom to ask. You can find the rest of the book, meet the people who still tell it, and let them correct you if you've got it wrong.
That's also why this path never blends sources into one teaching.
Blending is easy, and it sounds wise, but it erases the people. A teaching with no address can't be visited.
So: Zeno, from Diogenes Laertius. Kisa Gotami, from the Buddhist commentaries. The Samaritan, from Luke.

how: Scholars, librarians and many religious communities keep careful attributions and chains of transmission; in Islam, for example, each hadith is carried with its chain of narrators, and in Jewish study, teachings are traditionally quoted in the name of the one who said them.

o: a Sufi dancer who whirled in Rumi's circle
a Persian king who built libraries for poets
the Sufi writer who kept the stories of Rabia

games.q: which home kept which story — tap the pairs.

s: every quote signed Buddha online is from a Buddhist text
some appear in no Buddhist text at all.
the popular wording of the Rumi field line is a modern English version
beautiful, but not a translation you can check line by line.
blending all sources into one teaching honors them
it erases the people who kept them. this path names each home.

games.q: you find a lovely quote online, signed Buddha. you want to share it. what does this path do?
o: share it; it sounds like him
look for where it came from first
change the name to ancient wisdom
games.why: look for where it came from. if it's in a text, name the text. if you can't find it, say so, or don't sign it with his name.

practice: Pick one story from these weeks that stayed with you and name its home: the Stoics, the Zen teachers, the Taoists, the Jewish sages, the Sufis, the desert monks, the Buddhists, the Confucians, the Sikhs, the Christians, the old Greek fable-tellers.
Picture the people who kept it alive, generation after generation, so it could reach you. Silently, and by name, thank them.

wordCard.voice: Attar, the Sufi writer who kept the stories of Rabia: naming a source is honesty, gratitude, and a map back home. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a teaching with no address can't be visited. And when you don't know the address, it's honest to say so. Day ninety-five, done.
